title: Hillel on the Roof
summary: Young Hillel was very poor, but he wanted to learn Torah more than anything. One evening, when he had no money to get into the house of study, he climbed onto the roof and listened through the skylight, even when the snow began to fall. A story about loving to learn, never giving up, and teachers who cared for their student.
pages: In Jerusalem, a very, very long time ago, there lived a young man named Hillel. He had come from Babylon, far, far away, and he was very poor. His clothes were plain, and his sandals were already a little torn. But he had something that money can't buy: a heart that loved to learn.

Every morning Hillel went out to work. He carried things, cleaned and helped people, and at the end of the day he got one small coin, called a "tarpeik." He gave half the coin to the guard of the house of study, so he would let him in to learn. With the other half he bought bread for himself and his family.

In the house of study sat two great sages, Shemaya and Avtalyon. They taught Torah, and Hillel sat and listened, asked questions and listened again. Every word was to him like a slice of warm bread on a cold day. He didn't want to miss even one word.

One day, on a Friday, Hillel looked for work from morning until evening, and found none. There wasn't a single coin in his pocket. When he reached the house of study, the guard stood at the door and said, "No payment, no entry." The door closed, and Hillel was left outside.

Hillel looked up at the building. From inside came the voices of learning. "I must hear," he thought. Carefully he climbed up the wall, onto the roof, and lay down by the skylight, a little window in the ceiling. From there he could hear every word that Shemaya and Avtalyon said.

It was the month of Tevet, in the middle of winter. The wind blew, and Hillel's nose froze. And then white flakes began to fall: snow! But Hillel didn't move. He listened and listened, and forgot about the cold. The snow fell and fell, and slowly, slowly it covered him like a white, cold blanket.

In the morning, on Shabbat, Shemaya and Avtalyon sat in the house of study. Shemaya looked up and said, "Avtalyon, my dear friend, every day this room is bright, and today it is dark. Maybe it's cloudy today?" They looked up at the window in the ceiling, and saw there... the shape of a person!

They hurried up to the roof. There, under deep snow, almost as tall as a child, lay young Hillel, frozen with cold. Gently they brought him down, brushed off the snow, washed him in warm water and rubbed him with oil, so he would warm up.

Then they sat him beside a warm fire. But wait, it's Shabbat, and on Shabbat we don't light a fire! The sages said, "This one is worth breaking Shabbat for."
That means: for a young man like this, who loves Torah so much, and to save his life, it is allowed, and even right, to light a fire on Shabbat.

Slowly Hillel's cheeks turned pink, and his fingers grew warm. He smiled, and the sages smiled back at him. Young Hillel kept on learning, grew up, and became one of the greatest sages of the Jewish people: Hillel the Elder.

Do you also have something you love very much, something you're willing to work hard for? Maybe drawing, maybe a ball, maybe a question that won't let you rest. When you truly love something, you find a way, even if you have to climb a little. Just please, don't forget your coat.
